newsitem.title: USA: Dole primed for hard-hitting attack in final debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole primed for hard-hitting attack in final debate.

text.p: Republican challenger Bob Dole geared up for a two-fisted attack on President Bill Clinton's ethical record in a final debate on Wednesday less than three weeks before the election.

Dole was to visit the Shiley Theatre debate site during a day otherwise devoted to final cramming for a showdown he clearly needs to win. His aides, seeking to lower expectations for their candidate, said Clinton was going into the debate "a prohibitive favourite."
The debate is vital for Dole, who still lags behind his Democratic rival by double digits in polls tracking public opinion ahead of the Nov. 5 election.

The former senator delivered on Tuesday what could be a preview of his strategy in the final face-off with Clinton at the University of San Diego (9 p.m. EDT/0100 GMT) before a national television audience.

"No administration has been more self-righteous," Dole told a business audience. "But few administrations have been more self-serving. No administration has shown more arrogance. But few have displayed more ethical failures."

Clinton, who rehearsed for the debates in New Mexico, dismissed Dole's tongue-lashing as just politics, but Clinton campaign press secretary Joe Lockhart said Dole's remarks showed "the attack dog has been unleashed," referring to criticism of Dole in earlier campaigns as meanspirited.

In his speech on Tuesday, Dole counted off a series problems that have faced the Democratic White House including "more than 30 Clinton officials investigated, fired, or forced to resign due to ethical improprieties."

Dole has rarely made direct reference to the Whitewater investigation of a land deal Clinton and his wife, Hillary, invested in when they lived in Arkansas. But on Tuesday he again demanded that Clinton "should clearly promise there will be no (presidential) pardons in legal cases that personally concern him," alluding to Clinton's convicted Whitewater partners, Susan and James McDougal.
Former Iran-Contra special prosecutor Lawrence Walsh said in morning television talk shows on Wednesday that Dole's call for no pardons was "hypocrisy."

Walsh, who during the Reagan administration investigated the secret arms sales to Iran to finance arms for Nicaragua "Contra" rebels, said Dole was "the foremost advocate" of a pardon for former Defence Secretary Caspar Weinberger.

Walsh, who has been writing a book, "Firewall: The Iran-Contra Conspiracy and Cover-up," said in a statement that Dole lobbied then-President George Bush to pardon Weinberger ahead of his trial on charges related to the affair. Bush did pardon Weinberger.
"Senator Dole's demand that President Clinton forego future pardons connected with Whitewater gives the voters a remarkable view of Dole's hypocrisy ...." Walsh said.

Wednesday's debate will be set up as a town meeting, with questions posed by an audience of undecided voters selected by a Gallup poll. The first debate in Hartford, Connecticut, was more traditional, with questions asked by a single moderator.

In that encounter, Dole was praised for his good humour but post-debate polls said people thought that Clinton clearly won the event. A debate between Dole's running mate, Jack Kemp, and Vice President Al Gore, last Wednesday went to Gore, according to polls after that meeting.
